After sorting these pairs are (first, last), (second, second last), ... and the answer is the biggest of their sums. Sorting costs O(n log n).

problems.title: Fewest Cuts Into Palindromes
problems.statement:
Cut the text `text` into **pieces of consecutive letters** (together they must give back the whole text, in order) so that **every piece is a palindrome** (reads the same forwards and backwards). A single letter is a palindrome.

Return the **smallest number of cuts** needed. A text that is already a palindrome needs `0` cuts.

examples.explanation: aba | c | d: two cuts, three pieces. One cut is not enough: no split into two palindromes exists.
The whole text is a palindrome.

hints.nudge: Let cuts[i] be the fewest cuts for the first i letters. The last piece of that prefix is some palindrome that ends at letter i. How can you use this?
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming over prefixes: cuts[i] = min over palindromes text[j .. i - 1] of cuts[j] + 1; find all palindromes quickly by expanding around every centre.
hints.pseudocode:
cuts[i] = i - 1 for i in 0 .. n   (every letter alone; cuts[0] = -1 so that a whole-prefix palindrome costs 0)
for each centre c (a letter, then a gap between two letters):
  l = r = c (or l = c, r = c + 1); while l >= 0 and r < n and text[l] == text[r]:
    cuts[r + 1] = min(cuts[r + 1], cuts[l] + 1); l -= 1; r += 1
return cuts[n]
hints.walkthrough: Trying every set of cut positions is 2^(n-1). The last piece of the first i letters is a palindrome text[j .. i - 1]; the letters before it are cut in cuts[j] ways, so cuts[i] = min over such j of cuts[j] + 1 (and 0 if the whole prefix is a palindrome, which the trick cuts[0] = -1 handles automatically). Checking whether each text[j .. i - 1] is a palindrome naively makes it O(n^3). Instead of testing, GENERATE the palindromes: every palindrome grows from a centre (one letter for odd length, a gap between two letters for even length) by comparing the letters on both sides. Whenever the expansion covers text[l .. r], update cuts[r + 1] with cuts[l] + 1. Process the centres from left to right so that cuts[l] is final when it is used. There are 2n - 1 centres and each expansion is at most n long: O(n^2).

problems.title: Fewest Refuelling Stops
problems.statement:
A car drives along a straight road from position `0` to position `target`. It uses **1 unit of fuel per 1 unit of distance** and starts with `start_fuel` units. Each entry `[position, fuel]` in `stations` is a fuel station at that position that gives **all** of its `fuel` units if you stop there. The stations are listed in increasing order of position, and every position is between `1` and `target - 1`.

The tank has no size limit. You may refuel at a station you reach with an empty tank, and arriving at `target` with an empty tank counts as arriving. Return the **smallest number of stops** needed to reach `target`, or `-1` if it cannot be done.
constraints: 1 <= fuel <= 1000000000 for every station; positions are strictly increasing
sums can exceed a 32-bit integer: use 64-bit numbers

examples.explanation: Stop at 8 (fuel 20) and at 30 (fuel 25): the car can then reach 8 + ... in all 12 + 20 + 25 = 57 >= 50. One stop is not enough: 12 + 20 = 32 < 50.
Even using both stations the car can drive only 10 + 3 + 2 = 15 units.

hints.nudge: You do not have to decide at a station whether to stop. What if you could decide LATER, looking back at all the stations you passed?
hints.pattern: Greedy with a max-heap: drive as far as the fuel allows, remembering the fuel of every station you pass; when you get stuck, 'retroactively' refuel at the passed station with the most fuel.
hints.pseudocode:
reach = start_fuel; stops = 0; i = 0; heap = empty max-heap
while reach < target:
  push the fuel of every station with position <= reach (advance i)
  if heap is empty: return -1
  reach += pop the largest fuel; stops += 1
return stops
hints.walkthrough: A DP over (stop count -> furthest reach) works in O(n^2). A faster idea: `reach` is how far you can drive with what you have taken so far. All stations at or before `reach` are stations you could have stopped at. When `reach` is not yet the target, you must have refuelled once more, and to get the furthest you should have used the passed station with the MOST fuel. A max-heap holds the fuel of the stations you passed and have not used. Repeat: add every newly reachable station to the heap, take the largest, add it to `reach`, count one stop. If the heap is empty while `reach` is still short of the target, you are stuck: return -1. Use 64-bit numbers for `reach`.

problems.title: Smallest in a Rotated List
problems.statement:
A list of **different** numbers was sorted from smallest to largest and then **rotated** (cut at some position, with the two parts swapped), so `[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7]` can become `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`. It may also be left unrotated.

Return the **smallest number** in `nums`.
constraints: nums is a sorted list that was rotated by some amount

examples.explanation: The list was [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] rotated.
Not rotated: the first value is the smallest.

hints.nudge: Compare the middle element with the last one. What does it tell you about where the smallest number is?
hints.pattern: Binary search toward the rotation point.
hints.pseudocode:
lo = 0; hi = n - 1
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2
  if nums[mid] > nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1   // the drop is to the right of mid
  else: hi = mid                           // mid could be the smallest
return nums[lo]
hints.walkthrough: Taking the minimum of everything is O(n). The smallest value sits right after the 'drop' where the list falls from a large number to a small one. If nums[mid] is greater than nums[hi], the drop is somewhere to the right of mid, so the minimum is in (mid, hi]. Otherwise the part from mid to hi is sorted, so the minimum is at mid or to its left. Narrow the range until one element is left.

problems.title: Smallest Number in a Rotated List With Repeats
problems.statement:
A list that was sorted in **non-decreasing** order (equal values are allowed) has been **rotated**: some number of elements were moved from the front to the back, keeping their order. For example `[0, 1, 2, 2, 5]` rotated by 3 gives `[2, 5, 0, 1, 2]`.

Return the **smallest value** in the rotated list, doing better than looking at every element whenever the repeats allow it. The list is not empty.

examples.explanation: The sorted list [0, 1, 2, 2, 2] was rotated; the smallest value is 0.
The sorted list [1, 3, 3, 3] was rotated by 2; the smallest value is 1.

expected.time: O(log n) typical, O(n) worst case

hints.nudge: Compare the middle element with the LAST element. What does each of the three outcomes (smaller, larger, equal) tell you about where the smallest value is?
hints.pattern: Binary search against the right end: middle larger than the last means the minimum is to the right; middle smaller means it is at the middle or to the left; equal means you cannot tell, so drop only the last element.
hints.pseudocode:
lo = 0; hi = n - 1
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2
  if numbers[mid] > numbers[hi]: lo = mid + 1
  elif numbers[mid] < numbers[hi]: hi = mid
  else: hi = hi - 1
return numbers[lo]
hints.walkthrough: Without repeats, comparing the middle with the last element is decisive: if the middle is larger, the 'drop' where values fall lies to its right, so the minimum is right of mid; if it is smaller, the right part mid..hi is sorted and the minimum is at mid or to its left. With repeats there is a third case: middle equal to last. Then the minimum could be on either side (compare [1, 1, 1, 0, 1] and [1, 0, 1, 1, 1]), so you cannot throw half away. What you CAN do safely is discard the last element: its value is also present at mid (or the last element IS the minimum, but then the equal value at mid still gives the same answer). This makes the search O(log n) for most inputs but O(n) when almost everything is equal. Stopping when lo == hi leaves the answer at numbers[lo].

problems.title: Cheapest Way to Connect Everything
problems.statement:
A town has `nodes` villages numbered `0` to `nodes - 1`. Each entry `[a, b, cost]` in `roads` is a possible two-way road between villages `a` and `b` that costs `cost` to build.

Choose some of the roads so that **every village can reach every other village**, and make the total cost as small as possible. Return that smallest total cost, or `-1` if the villages cannot all be connected.
constraints: a and b are different villages; the same pair may appear more than once with different costs

examples.explanation: Build 0-1 (1), 1-2 (2) and 2-3 (4): 7. The road 0-2 is not needed.
Village 2 has no road at all.

hints.nudge: Which single road should definitely be built if it does not create a loop? Think about the cheapest road of all.
hints.pattern: Kruskal's algorithm: look at roads from cheapest to most expensive and keep a road only if it joins two villages that are not yet connected (Union-Find).
hints.pseudocode:
sort roads by cost
parent[i] = i; total = 0; joined = 0
for each road (a, b, cost) in that order:
  if find(a) != find(b): union them; total += cost; joined += 1
return total if joined == nodes - 1 else -1
hints.walkthrough: To connect n villages you need exactly n - 1 roads and never a loop. Trying all sets of n - 1 roads is hopeless. Greedy works here: take the roads in order of cost; a road is useful only if its two ends are not yet connected through roads you already chose, otherwise it would make a loop and only add cost. Union-Find tells you in almost constant time whether two villages are already connected and merges their groups when you choose a road. After going through all roads, if you chose n - 1 of them the villages are connected and the total is the answer; if fewer, some village cannot be reached, so return -1. The sort dominates: O(E log E). One village alone costs 0.

problems.title: A Stack That Knows Its Minimum
constraints: each push value is between 1 and 1000000000; the other operations are 0 and -1

examples.explanation: Push 5, push 3, minimum is 3; pop the 3, minimum is 5; pop the 5, the stack is empty so the report is 0.
The first report is on an empty stack. After pushing 2 twice the minimum is 2; after one pop it is still 2.

hints.nudge: When you pop the top, the minimum may change. What information could you have saved at the time of the push so that the pop can restore it?
hints.pattern: Keep a second stack that holds, for every entry of the main stack, the minimum of the stack up to and including that entry.
hints.pseudocode:
values = empty; mins = empty
for op in ops:
  if op > 0: push op on values; push min(op, mins.top if any) on mins
  elif op == 0: if values not empty: pop both
  else: report mins.top if any, else 0
hints.walkthrough: Searching the whole stack for the minimum at each report is O(n) per report. Instead store the answer in advance: next to every pushed value keep the minimum of everything that is in the stack at that moment, which is min(the new value, the previous stored minimum). The stored minimum of the top entry is then always the current minimum of the stack. Pop removes the value and its stored minimum together, which automatically brings back the previous minimum. A report is just a look at the top of the second stack (0 if the stack is empty). Everything is O(1) per operation, O(n) in total.

problems.title: Shortest Stretch to Reach a Total
problems.statement:
Every day a savings jar receives the amount `deposits[i]` (always positive). You want to reach at least `target` coins using a **stretch of consecutive days**.

Return the **fewest days** in a stretch whose deposits add up to **at least** `target`, or `0` if no stretch is enough.

examples.explanation: The days 4 and 3 add up to 7.
All the deposits together are only 3.

hints.nudge: Because deposits are positive, adding a day only increases the total and removing a day only decreases it.
hints.pattern: Two pointers: grow the right end until you reach the target, then shrink the left end as long as you still do.
hints.pseudocode:
left = 0; sum = 0; best = infinity
for right in 0..n-1:
  sum += deposits[right]
  while sum >= target: best = min(best, right - left + 1); sum -= deposits[left]; left++
return best or 0
hints.walkthrough: Checking every start and end is O(n^2). With positive numbers you can use a sliding window: extend the right end until the sum reaches the target, then record the length and move the left end forward while the sum still reaches the target (each move can only shorten the window). Both pointers only move forward, so O(n) total. If best was never updated return 0.

problems.title: Smallest Covering Window
problems.statement:
You have a long `text` and a short word `need`. A **window** is a stretch of consecutive letters of `text`. A window **covers** `need` if it contains every letter of `need`, as many times as that letter appears in `need` (extra letters in the window are fine).

Return the **length of the shortest window that covers `need`**, or `0` if no window does.
constraints: both strings contain only lowercase letters a-z

examples.explanation: The window banc contains a, b and c.
The text has only one a, but two are needed.

hints.nudge: Grow a window to the right until it covers `need`. Then, how can you make it smaller without breaking it?
hints.pattern: Sliding window with letter counts: expand the right end, then shrink the left end while the window still covers.
hints.walkthrough: Checking every window is O(n^2) windows times a check. Use two pointers. Keep a table of how many of each letter are still needed (it can go negative for extras) and a counter 'missing' of letters not yet covered. Move right one letter at a time. Whenever missing reaches 0 the window covers need: record its length, then move left forward to try to shrink it (if you remove a letter that was needed, missing goes up again and you stop shrinking). Each pointer moves at most n times, so O(n).

problems.title: The Shortest Stretch That Hides a Word
problems.statement: Find the **shortest contiguous substring** of `s` that contains `t` as a **subsequence** (the letters of `t` appear inside the substring in the same order, possibly with other letters between them). Return the **length** of that substring, or `0` if there is none. If `t` is empty the answer is `0`.
constraints: s and t contain lowercase letters

examples.explanation: The stretch aybzc (positions 1 to 5) contains a, b, c in order. No shorter stretch does.
The letter d does not occur.

hints.nudge: If you know where a matching stretch ENDS (the last letter of t is matched there), how would you find the best START for that end?
hints.pattern: Scan forward to the first position where all of t has been matched in order (this gives an end); then scan BACKWARDS from that end matching t from its last letter to its first to find the latest possible start; record the length and continue the search from just after that start.
hints.pseudocode:
i = 0
while i < len(s):
  j = 0; k = i; while k < len(s) and j < len(t): if s[k] == t[j]: j += 1; k += 1
  if j < len(t): break               (no further match)
  end = k - 1; j = len(t) - 1; k = end
  while j >= 0: if s[k] == t[j]: j -= 1; k -= 1
  start = k + 1; best = min(best, end - start + 1)
  i = start + 1
hints.walkthrough: Trying every start and growing the end (checking the subsequence each time) is O(n^2 * m). Better: a greedy forward scan matches the letters of t one after another and stops at the earliest end that completes t. But the start of the window found this way is not necessarily the tightest: walk back from the end, matching t from its last letter to its first, and the position where you finish is the LATEST start for that end; the window between them is the shortest one ending there. Record its length. Then restart the forward scan from start + 1 (a window starting at the same start would only find the same or a longer one). Each round costs at most the length of the window, and the windows overlap only a little, so the total is O(n * m) in the worst case.

problems.title: Mini Sudoku Completions
problems.statement:
A mini sudoku is a 4 by 4 grid that must be filled with the digits `1` to `4` so that every **row**, every **column** and each of the four **2 by 2 boxes** (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right) contains each digit exactly once.

`board` is a partly filled mini sudoku: `0` means an empty cell, and the digits that are already there never conflict with each other. Return the number of ways to fill the empty cells so that the whole board is valid. The answer can be `0`.
constraints: the given digits do not repeat in any row, column or box

examples.explanation: An empty mini sudoku has exactly 288 solutions.
Nothing is empty and the board is already valid: there is one way (do nothing).

hints.nudge: Fill the empty cells one after another. For one cell, which of the digits 1 to 4 are still allowed?
hints.pattern: Backtracking over the empty cells: place a legal digit, count the ways to finish, remove the digit, try the next one.
hints.pseudocode:
fill(i):
  if every empty cell is filled: return 1
  (r, c) = the i-th empty cell; total = 0
  for digit 1..4:
    if the digit is not in row r, column c or the box of (r, c):
      place it; total += fill(i + 1); remove it
  return total
hints.walkthrough: List the empty cells in reading order. Work through them with recursion: for the current cell try each digit 1 to 4 that does not already appear in its row, its column or its 2 by 2 box. After placing a digit, count the ways to fill the rest; then take the digit away again (backtracking) so that the next digit gets a clean board. Reaching the end of the list means every cell has a legal digit, which is exactly one valid completion. Add up the counts of all branches. Checking 'is this digit in the row, column or box' by scanning costs a few steps; keeping one small bitmask per row, column and box makes each check a single AND. The box of cell (r, c) has number (r / 2) * 2 + (c / 2). Most branches die quickly, so even the empty board needs only a few hundred steps.

problems.title: Fewest Swaps to Sort
problems.statement: `numbers` contains **different** numbers. In one **swap** you exchange the numbers at any two positions. Return the **smallest number of swaps** after which the list is sorted in increasing order.

examples.explanation: Swap the 4 with the 1 and the 3 with the 2.
The numbers 2, 3, 1 sit in a ring of three wrong places: two swaps fix it (swap 2 and 1: [1, 3, 2]; swap 3 and 2: [1, 2, 3]).

hints.nudge: Every number has a place where it belongs in the sorted list. Follow a number to its place, then the number that is there to ITS place, and so on. What shape do these chains have?
hints.pattern: Cycles of the permutation: a cycle of length L needs L - 1 swaps, so the answer is n minus the number of cycles.
hints.pseudocode:
target[i] = the position the number at i has in the sorted list
visited = all false; cycles = 0
for i in 0 .. n - 1: if not visited[i]: cycles += 1; walk j = i, then target[j], ... marking everything visited until you return to i
return n - cycles
hints.walkthrough: Compute for every position where its number must end up (sort the numbers and remember each one's index). Following 'this number goes to position p; the number currently at p goes to position q; ...' always returns to the start, so the positions split into separate rings (cycles). A number that is already in place is a ring of length 1 and needs no swap. A ring of length L can be fixed with L - 1 swaps (each swap puts one number into its final place), and no fewer, because one swap can only merge two rings or split one ring into two. So the minimum number of swaps is n - (number of rings). Sorting to find the target positions costs O(n log n).

problems.title: Mirror Tree
problems.statement:
A binary tree is **symmetric** (a mirror of itself) if its left half is the mirror image of its right half: the same shape and the same values when one half is flipped left to right.

Return `true` if the tree with the given `root` is symmetric. An empty tree is symmetric.

examples.explanation: Left child 2 has children 3 and 4; right child 2 has children 4 and 3: the right half is the left half flipped.
Both 2s have their only child on the right side, so flipping one half does not give the other.

hints.nudge: Instead of looking at the tree as a whole, look at TWO nodes at once. Which two nodes have to match for the tree to be a mirror?
hints.pattern: Recursion on a pair of nodes: the outside children must match each other and the inside children must match each other.
hints.walkthrough: A tree is a mirror when its left subtree and its right subtree are mirror images of each other. Define a helper that compares two nodes a and b which are supposed to be mirror images: if both are missing, they match; if only one is missing, they do not; otherwise their values must be equal AND a's left side must mirror b's right side AND a's right side must mirror b's left side. Start with the root's two children (an empty tree, or a tree with just a root, is symmetric). Every node is looked at once: O(n) time, and the recursion depth is the height of the tree.

problems.title: Missing Number
problems.statement:
A box should contain tickets numbered `0, 1, 2, ..., n`, but one ticket is lost, so only `n` tickets are left in `numbers`, all different.

Return the **number of the lost ticket**.
constraints: numbers contains n different values taken from 0..n, where n = len(numbers)

examples.explanation: The tickets 0..3 should all be there; 2 is missing.
0 and 1 are present, so the lost ticket is the last one, 2.

hints.nudge: You know exactly which numbers should be there. What is their total?
hints.pattern: Compare an expected total with the actual total.
hints.pseudocode:
expected = n * (n + 1) / 2
return expected - sum(numbers)
hints.walkthrough: Checking each possible ticket against the whole list is O(n^2). The numbers 0..n add up to n*(n+1)/2. The list contains all of them except one, so the missing ticket is the expected total minus the actual total of the list. One pass, O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Largest Number With Rising Digits
problems.statement:
A number has **rising digits** if, reading its digits from left to right, each digit is **greater than or equal to** the digit before it (`1234`, `1334` and `7` qualify; `332` does not).

Given a whole number `number`, return the **largest number that is at most `number`** and has rising digits.

examples.explanation: 332 does not rise (3, 3, 2). No number from 300 to 332 rises, and 299 does.
Already rising.

hints.nudge: Find the first place where the digits stop rising. Making just that digit smaller is not enough: what happens to the digits after it?
hints.pattern: Greedy on the digits: from the right, whenever a digit is smaller than the one before it, lower the earlier digit by 1 and remember that every digit from there on can become 9.
hints.pseudocode:
digits = the digits of number; mark = number of digits
for i from last down to 1:
  if digits[i - 1] > digits[i]: digits[i - 1] -= 1; mark = i
set every digit from position mark to the end to 9
return the number written by the digits
hints.walkthrough: Subtracting 1 until the digits rise works for small numbers but needs up to a billion steps for big ones. Look at the digits instead. If they already rise, the number is its own answer. Otherwise some digit is larger than the digit to its right (in 332 the second 3 is larger than the 2). To get below the number you must lower such a digit by 1, and then every digit to its right can be 9, which keeps the number as large as possible. But lowering a digit can make it smaller than the digit on ITS left (in 332 the second 3 becomes 2, which is smaller than the first 3), so the repair has to continue to the left. Scan from the right to the left: whenever a digit is larger than its right neighbour, subtract 1 from it and remember its right neighbour's position. At the end set every digit from the leftmost remembered position to the last one to 9. For 332: the second 3 becomes 2 (position 2 remembered), then the first 3 becomes 2 (position 1 remembered), and the digits from position 1 on become 9: 299. This takes one pass over the digits.

problems.title: The Most Valuable Truck Load
problems.statement:
A warehouse has several kinds of boxes. `boxes[i] = [count, units]` means there are `count` identical boxes of kind `i`, and each of them holds `units` units of goods. The truck can carry **at most `truck_size` boxes** in total (all boxes are the same size, whatever they hold).

Choose the boxes to load so that the **total number of units** on the truck is as large as possible, and return that total.

examples.explanation: Take the one box of 5 units, then the two boxes of 3 units, then one box of 1 unit: 5 + 6 + 1 = 12.
Only one kind of box; the truck takes 3 of the 5 boxes.

hints.nudge: Every box takes the same room on the truck. Which boxes would you load first?
hints.pattern: Greedy: sort the kinds of boxes by units per box, largest first, and take as many boxes of each kind as still fit.
hints.pseudocode:
sort boxes by units, largest first
room = truck_size; total = 0
for each kind (count, units): take = min(count, room); total += take * units; room -= take; stop when room is 0
return total
hints.walkthrough: All boxes use the same space, so the only thing that matters is how much each one holds. If a box with fewer units is on the truck while a box with more units stays behind, swapping them gives a better load, so the best load always takes the most valuable boxes first. Sort the kinds by units per box, largest first; for each kind take as many boxes as are available and as still fit (min of the count and the remaining room), add take * units to the total and reduce the room. Stop when the truck is full or the kinds run out. Sorting is O(n log n); the load itself is O(n).

problems.title: Find the Peak
problems.statement:
`heights` describes a mountain trail: the heights **strictly increase up to one peak and then strictly decrease** (so there are at least 3 values, and the peak is never the first or last one).

Return the **index of the peak**.
constraints: heights strictly increases and then strictly decreases

examples.explanation: 2 is the highest and sits at index 1.
The peak is 10.

hints.nudge: Look at the middle element and the one after it. Are you going uphill or downhill there?
hints.pattern: Binary search on the slope: compare heights[mid] with heights[mid + 1].
hints.pseudocode:
lo = 0; hi = n - 1
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2
  if heights[mid] < heights[mid + 1]: lo = mid + 1   // still climbing: peak is to the right
  else: hi = mid                                      // descending: peak is at mid or to the left
return lo
hints.walkthrough: A scan for the maximum is O(n). On this trail, if heights[mid] < heights[mid + 1] you are on the way up, so the peak is to the right of mid. Otherwise you are on the way down (or at the peak), so the peak is at mid or to its left. Keep shrinking the range; when it has one element left, that is the peak. O(log n).

problems.title: A Stretch That Adds Up to a Multiple
problems.statement:
Is there a **contiguous stretch of at least 2 numbers** in `numbers` whose sum is a **multiple of `k`**? The sum `0` counts as a multiple of `k`.

Return `true` if there is one, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: The stretch 4, 6 adds up to 10, a multiple of 5.
All stretches of two or more numbers add up to 6, 10, 11, 15, 12 and 17: none is a multiple of 7.

hints.nudge: The sum of a stretch is a difference of two prefix sums. When is a difference of two numbers a multiple of k?
hints.pattern: Prefix sums modulo k stored in a hash map: two equal remainders with at least one number between them mean a stretch whose sum is a multiple of k.
hints.pseudocode:
first = { 0: -1 }; total = 0
for i, x in numbers:
  total = (total + x) mod k
  if total in first:
    if i - first[total] >= 2: return true
  else: first[total] = i
return false
hints.walkthrough: Checking all stretches is O(n^2). Let P(i) be the running sum up to position i. The sum of the stretch after position a up to position b is P(b) - P(a), and it is a multiple of k exactly when P(a) and P(b) have the SAME remainder modulo k. So keep a map from remainder to the EARLIEST position where that remainder was seen (start with remainder 0 at position -1, for stretches that begin at the start). For each position compute the new remainder; if it was seen before at position a and the stretch is long enough (b - a >= 2), return true. If it was seen but the stretch would have length 1, keep the earlier position (a longer stretch is easier to get later). Taking the remainder as you go keeps the numbers small. O(n).

problems.title: Multiply Two Big Numbers
problems.statement:
Two non-negative whole numbers are given as **texts of digits** (no leading zeros, except the number `0` itself). Return their **product**, also as a text of digits.

The numbers can be hundreds of digits long, far too big for a normal integer, so work digit by digit like multiplication on paper.
constraints: digits only, no leading zeros except the single digit 0

hints.nudge: On paper, multiplying digit i of one number by digit j of the other adds something to ONE column of the answer. Which column?
hints.pattern: An array of n + m digit slots: digit i times digit j goes into slot i + j + 1 (and its carry into slot i + j), counting from the left.
hints.pseudocode:
if either number is '0': return '0'
result = array of n + m zeros
for i from n-1 down to 0:
  for j from m-1 down to 0:
    total = digit(first[i]) * digit(second[j]) + result[i + j + 1]
    result[i + j + 1] = total mod 10
    result[i + j] += total / 10
skip leading zeros of the result and join the digits
hints.walkthrough: A product of an n-digit and an m-digit number has at most n + m digits, so prepare that many slots, all 0. The digit at position i (from the left) of the first number has place value 10^(n-1-i), and the digit at position j of the second has 10^(m-1-j), so their product belongs to the place value 10^(n+m-2-i-j), which is slot i + j + 1 counted from the left (and the carry goes one slot further left, i + j). Multiply every pair, add the product to the slot's current content, keep one digit in the slot and push the carry to the left slot. The slots always stay small enough to carry later. At the end remove the leading zeros (the product has n + m or n + m - 1 digits). Handle zero separately so that you return `0`, not `00`. O(n * m).

problems.title: Peaceful Queens
problems.statement:
On an `n` by `n` chessboard you want to place `n` queens so that **no two queens attack each other**. A queen attacks every square in its own row, its own column, and along both diagonals.

Return the **number of different ways** to place the `n` queens.

examples.explanation: A 4 x 4 board has exactly two peaceful arrangements (mirror images of each other).
One queen on a 1 x 1 board.

hints.nudge: There must be exactly one queen in each row. So place them row by row. For each row, which columns are still safe?
hints.pattern: Backtracking: place a queen in the next row in any safe column, recurse, then undo.
hints.pseudocode:
place(row): if row == n: return 1
  total = 0
  for each column c that is not attacked (column, diagonal, anti-diagonal unused):
    mark c; total += place(row + 1); unmark c
  return total
hints.walkthrough: Trying every placement of n queens on n*n squares is hopeless, but one queen per row is forced, so place queens row by row. In each row try every column, skipping those attacked by the queens already placed: same column, same diagonal (row - col equal) or same anti-diagonal (row + col equal). Keep three sets (or bit masks) of used columns and diagonals so each check is O(1). When all n rows are filled, count one solution; then undo the last queen and try the next column (backtracking). The counts for n = 1..9 are 1, 0, 0, 2, 10, 4, 40, 92, 352.

problems.title: Nearby Duplicate
problems.statement:
A camera logs a number each second in `readings`. A repeat is **suspicious** if the same number appears at two different positions that are at most `k` apart.

Return `true` if there are two positions `i != j` with `readings[i] == readings[j]` and `|i - j| <= k`, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: The 1s are at positions 0 and 3, which are 3 apart.
Equal numbers are always 3 apart, which is more than 2.

hints.nudge: When you see a number, what single piece of information about its last appearance is enough?
hints.pattern: Hash map from value to its most recent index.
hints.walkthrough: Comparing every pair within distance k costs O(n*k). Scan once and remember, for each value, the index where you last saw it. If the current value was seen before and the gap i - last is at most k, you found a suspicious repeat. Otherwise update the last index to i (only the closest earlier copy matters). O(n) time.

problems.title: Is There a Money-Making Loop
problems.statement:
A directed graph has `n` nodes (`0` to `n - 1`). `edges[i] = [from, to, weight]` is a directed edge; the weight may be **negative**. A **cycle** is a path that starts and ends at the same node (a self-loop `[v, v, w]` is a cycle of one edge). Its weight is the sum of the weights of its edges.

Return `true` if the graph contains a cycle whose total weight is **negative** (less than 0), anywhere in the graph, otherwise `false`. A cycle of weight exactly `0` does not count.

examples.explanation: The loop 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 0 has weight 2 - 5 + 2 = -1.
The same loop has weight 0, which is not negative.

hints.nudge: Imagine you keep improving the shortest-distance estimates by following edges. In a graph without a negative cycle, how many rounds of improvement can there be at most? What happens if there is one?
hints.pattern: Bellman-Ford: start every distance at 0 (so every component is covered), relax all edges up to n times; if the distances still change in round n, a negative cycle exists.
hints.pseudocode:
dist = [0] * n
repeat n times:
  changed = false
  for (u, v, w) in edges: if dist[u] + w < dist[v]: dist[v] = dist[u] + w; changed = true
  if not changed: return false
return true
hints.walkthrough: Checking all cycles is exponential. The estimates dist[v] only ever go down. Without a negative cycle, a shortest path uses at most n - 1 edges, so after n - 1 rounds of 'relax every edge' nothing can improve any more, and round n changes nothing. With a negative cycle you can keep going around it and lowering the distances for ever, so the distances still change in every round. Starting all distances at 0 is like adding a hidden start node that has a zero-weight edge to every node: it makes cycles in any part of the graph reachable, even in nodes that are not connected to node 0. So run the rounds; if a round changes nothing, answer false; if all n rounds changed something, answer true. Floyd-Warshall gives the same answer (a negative number on the diagonal) in O(n^3).

problems.title: Next Greater on a Ring
problems.statement:
The numbers of `numbers` are arranged on a **ring**: after the last number comes the first one again. For every number, find the **first strictly greater** number you meet when you walk to the right (continuing around the ring if needed, but never more than one full circle). If there is none, the answer for that number is `-1`.

Return the answers in the original order.

examples.explanation: For the first 1 the next greater is 2. The 2 is the largest, so -1. For the last 1, walking right wraps around to the first 1 (not greater) and then 2.
For 4: after it come 1 and 2 (smaller), then the ring wraps to 3 (smaller) and 8. For the last 2 the first greater is the wrapped 3.

hints.nudge: A ring of n numbers is the same as a list of 2n numbers where the second half repeats the first. How does that help for the numbers near the end?
hints.pattern: Monotonic stack, scanned over the list twice (positions 0 to 2n - 1, using the position modulo n); answers are recorded only on the first lap.
hints.pseudocode:
answer = [-1] * n; stack = empty (holds positions)
for i in 0 .. 2n - 1:
  while stack not empty and numbers[stack.top] < numbers[i mod n]: answer[stack.pop()] = numbers[i mod n]
  if i < n: push i
return answer
hints.walkthrough: The straightforward way looks at up to n - 1 following numbers for each number: O(n^2). A stack holds the positions whose answer has not been found yet, always with non-increasing values from bottom to top. When a new number arrives, every waiting number on the stack that is smaller than it has just found its first greater number: pop them and record it. Because a number on a ring can find its answer in the wrapped-around part, run through the positions twice (0 to 2n - 1, reading numbers[i mod n]); only push new positions during the first lap, so that every position waits at most one full circle. Whatever is still on the stack at the end has no greater number: it stays -1. O(n).

problems.title: Next Arrangement
problems.statement:
Think of all the different ways to arrange the numbers of `nums`, listed in dictionary order (compare the first numbers, then the second, and so on). Return the arrangement that comes **right after** `nums` in that list.

If `nums` is already the last arrangement (the numbers are in descending order), wrap around and return the **first** arrangement (ascending order). The list can contain repeated numbers.

examples.explanation: After 1 2 3 comes 1 3 2.
3 2 1 is the last arrangement, so wrap around to the smallest.

hints.nudge: To get the NEXT arrangement you change as little as possible, so you change a digit as far to the right as you can.
hints.pattern: Find the last place where the sequence goes up, swap with the next larger value on its right, then reverse the tail.
hints.pseudocode:
i = n-2; while i >= 0 and nums[i] >= nums[i+1]: i--
if i >= 0:
  j = n-1; while nums[j] <= nums[i]: j--
  swap(nums[i], nums[j])
reverse(nums[i+1 .. n-1])
hints.walkthrough: Scan from the right for the first index i where nums[i] < nums[i+1]. Everything to the right of i is in descending order, i.e. already the largest possible arrangement of those numbers, so to go to the next arrangement you must increase position i. Choose the smallest number on the right that is still bigger than nums[i] (the rightmost one that is > nums[i], because the tail is descending), swap it with nums[i], then reverse the tail so it becomes the smallest possible (ascending). If no such i exists, the whole list is descending: reversing it gives the first arrangement.

problems.title: Binary Strings Without Twin Ones
problems.statement:
A binary string is made of the characters `0` and `1`. Count the binary strings of length exactly `n` that **never have two `1`s next to each other** (for example `0101` is fine, `0110` is not).

Return the number of such strings.

examples.explanation: 00, 01 and 10 (11 is not allowed).

hints.nudge: Build the string one character at a time. What does the last character you wrote decide about the next one?
hints.pattern: Backtracking: append 0 always, append 1 only when the last character is not 1. Then notice the same states repeat.
hints.pseudocode:
count(remaining, lastWasOne):
  if remaining == 0: return 1
  total = count(remaining - 1, false)          // put a 0
  if not lastWasOne: total += count(remaining - 1, true)   // put a 1
  return total
hints.walkthrough: Checking all 2^n strings works for small n only. Building the string character by character is faster because you never extend a string that already has two adjacent ones: a 0 can always be added, a 1 only after a 0 (or at the start). The number of completions depends only on how many characters remain and whether the last one was a 1, so remember those answers (memoization) or keep two running counts: strings ending in 0 and strings ending in 1. Each step: new_zero = zero + one, new_one = zero. The answer for n = 30 is 2178309.

problems.title: How Many Nodes Are K Steps Away
problems.statement:
All node values of a binary tree are **different**. `target` is the value of one node in the tree. The **distance** between two nodes is the number of edges on the path between them; the path may go **up** to a parent as well as down to children.

Return the number of nodes whose distance from the target node is **exactly `k`**.
constraints: values are different integers between 0 and 100000; `target` is the value of a node in the tree

examples.explanation: From 4 the path 4, 2, 1, 3, 6 (or 7) has 4 edges: the nodes 6 and 7.
The children of the root: 2 and 3.

hints.nudge: From the target you can walk DOWN easily, but a tree has no link to the parent. Which nodes above the target would you need to remember, and what is the distance to them?
hints.pattern: Either build parent links (or an undirected graph) and run a breadth-first search for k steps from the target; or a single recursion that returns the distance to the target and counts nodes in the 'other side' subtrees at the remaining distance.
hints.pseudocode:
BFS version: parent[node] = its parent; queue = [target node]; repeat k times: replace the queue by all unvisited neighbours (left, right, parent); return the size of the queue
Recursive version: go(node) returns the distance from node to the target if the target is in its subtree, else -1; on the way up count nodes of the opposite subtree at depth k - distance - 1
hints.walkthrough: Treat the tree as an undirected graph: every node is connected to its two children and its parent. Record the parent of each node in one traversal, locate the target node, then do a breadth-first search from the target for exactly k rounds, never visiting a node twice; the nodes in the queue after k rounds are exactly the nodes at distance k. In the recursive alternative, every node that has the target in its subtree at distance d from it (d < k) can reach nodes in its OTHER child's subtree at depth k - d - 1 below that child; the node itself is at distance k when d = k; and nodes below the target at depth k are counted when the target is found. Both versions visit each node a constant number of times: O(n).

problems.title: The N-th Number Divisible by A or B
problems.statement: A positive whole number is **magical** if it is divisible by `a` or by `b` (or both). Return the `n`-th smallest magical number, **modulo 1,000,000,007** (the number itself can be very large).

examples.explanation: The multiples of 4 or 6 are 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 18, ...: the 5th is 16.
a and b are equal: the magical numbers are the multiples of 2: 2, 4, 6.

hints.nudge: Suppose you pick a number x. Can you count how many magical numbers are at most x without listing them? Careful about numbers divisible by both.
hints.pattern: Binary search on the value x: count(x) = x / a + x / b - x / lcm(a, b) (inclusion-exclusion); find the smallest x with count(x) >= n.
hints.pseudocode:
l = lcm(a, b); lo = min(a, b); hi = n * min(a, b)
while lo < hi:
  mid = (lo + hi) / 2
  if mid / a + mid / b - mid / l >= n: hi = mid else: lo = mid + 1
return lo mod 1,000,000,007
hints.walkthrough: Generating the magical numbers one by one is O(n), far too slow for n = 10^9. Count instead. Up to x there are x / a multiples of a and x / b multiples of b (whole-number division), but the multiples of both (multiples of the lcm) are counted twice, so count(x) = x / a + x / b - x / lcm(a, b). This count grows with x, so binary search for the smallest x with count(x) >= n: it is magical (the count just reached n at x, so x must be a multiple of a or b). The answer is at most n * min(a, b), up to 4 * 10^13, so search with 64-bit numbers and reduce modulo 1,000,000,007 only at the end. (Another way: the pattern repeats every lcm(a, b) numbers, with a + b - gcd(a, b) magical numbers in each period.)

problems.title: The N-th Number Made of 2s, 3s and 5s
problems.statement:
A positive whole number is **smooth** if it has no prime factor other than `2`, `3` and `5` (so it can be written as `2^a * 3^b * 5^c`). The number `1` counts as smooth (all exponents are zero).

The smooth numbers in increasing order are `1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, ...` (7 is not smooth, 11 is not, 14 is not). Return the `n`-th one, counting from `1`.

examples.explanation: The first ten smooth numbers are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12.
The first one is 1.

expected.time: O(n log n) with a heap, O(n) with three pointers

hints.nudge: Every smooth number except 1 is a smaller smooth number multiplied by 2, 3 or 5. How can you produce the smooth numbers in increasing order from that fact?
hints.pattern: A min-heap of candidates (start with 1; pop the smallest x, push 2x, 3x and 5x, skipping numbers already seen). Or three pointers into the list built so far.
hints.pseudocode:
heap = [1]; seen = {1}
repeat n times:
  x = pop the smallest
  for p in 2, 3, 5: if x * p not in seen: add it to seen and push it
return the last x popped
hints.walkthrough: Testing every integer for smoothness (divide out 2s, 3s and 5s and see whether 1 is left) works but wastes time on the many numbers that are not smooth. Generate them instead. The smallest smooth number is 1. Whenever x is smooth, so are 2x, 3x and 5x, and every smooth number is reached this way from a smaller one. Keep a min-heap of the numbers found but not yet 'used': pop the smallest (this is the next smooth number in order), and push its three multiples. The same number can be produced in different ways (6 = 2 * 3 = 3 * 2), so remember what was already pushed in a set. After n pops the last popped value is the answer. A faster way keeps the list of smooth numbers found and three pointers (for the next multiple of 2, 3 and 5 to try): the next number is the smallest of the three candidates, and every pointer whose candidate was taken moves on.

problems.title: Equal Distances From One Point
problems.statement:
`points[i] = [x, y]` is a point on a plane (points may repeat). A **boomerang** is an **ordered** triple of different positions `(i, j, k)` such that the distance from point `i` to point `j` **equals** the distance from point `i` to point `k`. The order matters: `(i, j, k)` and `(i, k, j)` are two different boomerangs.

Return the number of boomerangs.

examples.explanation: From each corner of the square the two neighbouring corners are at the same distance (2): that is 2 ordered pairs per corner, 4 * 2 = 8.
One point cannot make a triple.

hints.nudge: Fix the point i, the 'centre'. For the other points only their distance from i matters. When do two other points j and k make a boomerang with i?
hints.pattern: For each centre count how many points lie at each (squared) distance; a group of c points at the same distance gives c * (c - 1) ordered pairs.
hints.walkthrough: Checking every triple costs O(n^3), about 10^8 steps for 500 points. Group instead by centre. For a fixed centre, two other points j and k form a boomerang exactly when they have the same distance from it. Use the SQUARED distance as the key (it is a whole number, so no rounding problems). If c points share one distance, you can choose the ordered pair (j, k) in c * (c - 1) ways. Summing this over the distances of one centre and then over all centres gives the answer in O(n^2). Points that repeat have distance 0 from each other, which is handled by the same rule.

problems.title: How Many Different Island Shapes
problems.statement:
`grid` is a map of `1` (land) and `0` (water). An **island** is a group of land cells connected through their sides (up, down, left, right). Two islands have the **same shape** if one can be moved onto the other **by sliding it** (translation) without rotating or flipping it.

Return the number of **different island shapes**.

examples.explanation: An L-shaped island of three cells and a vertical pair of cells: two different shapes.
Four single-cell islands all have the same shape.

hints.nudge: Two islands that are translations of each other have the same cells relative to their top-left corner. How could you write an island down so that equal shapes give equal descriptions?
hints.pattern: Find every island with a flood fill; describe it by the positions of its cells relative to its first cell (or by the path of the search); put the descriptions into a set; the answer is the size of the set.
hints.pseudocode:
shapes = empty set
for each unvisited land cell (r0, c0): collect the cells of its island with a flood fill
  shape = sorted list of (r - r0, c - c0) for every cell, where (r0, c0) is the first cell found in row-major order
  add shape to shapes
return the size of shapes
hints.walkthrough: Sliding an island does not change the offsets of its cells from a fixed reference cell. Scanning the grid row by row, the first land cell of an island you meet is its top-most (and, in that row, left-most) cell, which is the same part of the shape wherever the island lies. So record each cell as (row - row0, column - column0) relative to that cell. Sort the offsets (or collect them in the same order), turn the list into something you can store in a set (a tuple or a text), and add it. Rotated or mirrored copies produce different offset lists, which is exactly what the problem wants. Another way is to record the sequence of moves of the depth-first search, including a mark when it backtracks. O(rows * columns).

problems.title: Odd Positions First
problems.statement:
Number the nodes of a linked list `1, 2, 3, ...` from the head. Rearrange the list so that **all nodes at odd positions come first, then all nodes at even positions**, keeping the original order inside each group. Return the head.

Do it by re-linking the existing nodes, using only a constant amount of extra memory.

examples.explanation: Positions 1, 3, 5 hold 1, 3, 5; positions 2, 4 hold 2, 4.
Odd positions: 2, 3, 6, 7. Even positions: 1, 5, 4. The values themselves do not matter, only the positions.

hints.nudge: Build two chains at once while you walk along the list: one for the odd positions and one for the even positions. When you are done, how do the two chains join?
hints.pattern: Two pointers re-linking the list in place: odd.next skips over one node, even.next skips over one node; finally the odd chain's tail points to the head of the even chain.
hints.pseudocode:
if the list is empty: return empty
odd = head; even_head = even = head.next
while even and even.next:
  odd.next = even.next; odd = odd.next
  even.next = odd.next; even = even.next
odd.next = even_head
return head
hints.walkthrough: Remember where the even chain starts (the second node). Keep a pointer on the last odd node and a pointer on the last even node. In each round, the odd chain takes the node after the current even node (odd.next = even.next, then move odd), and the even chain takes the node after that (even.next = odd.next, then move even). Stop when the even pointer or its next is missing: then the odd chain has taken every odd-position node. Finally link the end of the odd chain to the start of the even chain. Make sure the last even node's next ends up empty: the loop's own updates handle that. No nodes are copied, so memory is O(1) and every node is touched once: O(n).

problems.title: Can One Change Fix the Order
problems.statement: Return `true` if you can make `numbers` **non-decreasing** (each number at least as big as the one before it) by **changing at most one number** to any value you like, otherwise `false`. A list that is already non-decreasing needs no change.

examples.explanation: Change the 2 into 5: the list becomes 3, 5, 5, 6, which is non-decreasing.
The 1 is too small after 6, and fixing it breaks the next pair; no single change helps.

hints.nudge: A problem can only appear where a number is bigger than the one after it. If this happens twice, can one change fix both?
hints.pattern: Scan for a 'descent' (numbers[i] > numbers[i + 1]); count descents, and at a descent decide which of the two numbers to change: lower the left one if it is safe for the number before it, otherwise raise the right one.
hints.walkthrough: Trying every position and every value is slow. A descent is a pair (i, i + 1) with numbers[i] > numbers[i + 1]; the list is sorted exactly when there is none. With two or more separate descents one change cannot help (usually), so count them. At the first descent you must change one of the two numbers. Lowering numbers[i] to numbers[i + 1] is the safer choice because it keeps the left part as small as it can be, but it is only allowed if the number before it is not larger than numbers[i + 1] (or there is no number before it). If it is not allowed, raise numbers[i + 1] to numbers[i] instead, and continue scanning with the changed list: the change may create a new descent right after it, which is then counted as a second change. Work on a copy.

problems.title: Exactly One Edit Apart
problems.statement: An **edit** is one of: inserting one letter, deleting one letter, or replacing one letter by a different one. Return `true` if `first` can be turned into `second` with **exactly one** edit, otherwise `false`. Two identical texts need zero edits, so for them the answer is `false`.
constraints: both texts use only lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: Delete the `a`.
The texts are identical: zero edits are needed, not one.

hints.nudge: How different can the lengths be if only one edit happened? And what does the position of the first difference tell you?
hints.pattern: Compare from the front until the first mismatch, then compare the REST of the texts in the way the edit type requires.
hints.walkthrough: Computing the full edit distance with a table works but costs O(n * m). One edit means the texts are almost the same. First the lengths: if they differ by more than 1 the answer is false. Let a be the shorter one. Move along both texts while the letters are equal and stop at the first mismatch i. If you reached the end of a without a mismatch, the texts are equal (false) or b has exactly one extra letter at the end (true). Otherwise decide by the lengths: with equal lengths the mismatching letters must be a replacement, so everything after position i must be equal; with different lengths b has an extra letter at position i, so a[i:] must equal b[i+1:]. One pass: O(n).

problems.title: Water That Reaches Both Oceans
problems.statement:
`heights[r][c]` is the height of the land in a cell. The left and the top edges of the map touch the **Pacific** ocean, the right and the bottom edges touch the **Atlantic** ocean. Rain water on a cell can flow to a neighbouring cell (up, down, left or right) if that neighbour is **not higher** (its height is less than or equal to the current cell's).

Water reaches an ocean when it flows off the edge that touches it. Count the cells from which water can flow to **both** oceans.

examples.explanation: Every cell can reach both oceans (for example the top-left 2 reaches the Atlantic through the 1 on its right, which lies on the right edge).
Water only flows towards the top-left (to lower cells), so it reaches the Atlantic only from cells that already lie on the bottom row or right column: 5 cells.

hints.nudge: Instead of asking, for every cell, where its water goes, ask the opposite: which cells can water reach the Pacific FROM? Start at the Pacific edge and walk uphill.
hints.pattern: Two reverse flood fills: from all Pacific-edge cells move to neighbours that are NOT LOWER (that is where the water came from); the same from the Atlantic edge; count the cells marked by both.
hints.pseudocode:
reach(startCells): mark startCells; stack = startCells
  while stack: cell = pop; for each neighbour not marked with height >= height[cell]: mark it; push it
  return the marked set
pacific = reach(top row + left column); atlantic = reach(bottom row + right column)
answer = number of cells in both sets
hints.walkthrough: Following the water downhill from every cell costs O((rows * columns)^2) in the worst case. Reverse the direction: water can come from a neighbour to a cell if the neighbour is at least as high. So starting from the cells at the Pacific edge, spread to neighbours that are not lower: those are exactly the cells whose water can flow (downhill or level) to the Pacific. Do the same for the Atlantic edge. A cell that is marked in both searches can send water to both oceans. Each search visits every cell at most once: O(rows * columns).

problems.title: Paint the Fence
problems.statement:
A fence has `posts` posts in a row and you have `colors` colors of paint. Every post gets exactly one color. The rule: **no three posts in a row may have the same color** (two in a row is fine).

Return the **number of different ways** to paint the fence.

examples.explanation: With 2 colors there are 8 ways to paint 3 posts, minus the 2 ways that use one color on all three.
Any pair of colors is allowed: 3 * 3.

hints.nudge: Look at the last two posts. Are they the same color or different? That decides what the next post may be.
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming with two counts: ways where the last two posts match, and ways where they differ.
hints.pseudocode:
same = colors; diff = colors * (colors - 1)      // after 2 posts
repeat posts - 2 times: (same, diff) = (diff, (same + diff) * (colors - 1))
return same + diff    // for posts == 1 the answer is just colors
hints.walkthrough: Count paintings by whether the last two posts have the same color. A new post can always get a color different from the previous post: (colors - 1) choices, from any painting. It can copy the previous post's color only if the previous two posts were different. So new_same = diff, new_diff = (same + diff) * (colors - 1). Start after two posts with same = colors and diff = colors * (colors - 1), and handle posts = 1 separately (the answer is colors). O(n) time. Checking all colors^posts paintings is only fine for tiny fences.

problems.title: Paint Region Size
problems.statement:
A picture is a grid of colour numbers. Two cells are in the same **region** when they have the same colour and you can walk from one to the other by moving up, down, left or right, only through cells of that colour.

Return how many cells are in the region that contains the cell at row `row`, column `col` (both counted from `0`).

examples.explanation: The 1s at (0,0), (0,1) and (1,0) are connected. The 1 at (2,2) is a different region: it touches no other 1.
The 0s at (0,2), (1,1), (1,2), (2,0) and (2,1) form one region.

hints.nudge: Start on the given cell. Which cells can you reach in one step, and which of those are allowed?
hints.pattern: Flood fill: a depth-first or breadth-first search that only walks onto cells of the same colour, and never visits a cell twice.
hints.pseudocode:
colour = grid[row][col]
seen = {(row, col)}; stack = [(row, col)]
while stack not empty:
  (r, c) = pop
  for each of the 4 neighbours (nr, nc) inside the grid:
    if not seen and grid[nr][nc] == colour: mark seen, push
return size of seen
hints.walkthrough: Remember the colour of the starting cell. Keep a stack (or queue) of cells whose neighbours still have to be looked at, and a set of cells already counted. Take a cell off the stack, look at its four neighbours, and for each neighbour that is inside the grid, has the same colour, and has not been counted yet, count it and put it on the stack. When the stack is empty, nothing else can be reached, and the number of counted cells is the answer. Marking a cell as counted when you PUSH it (not when you pop it) keeps a cell from being added twice. Each cell is handled once, so O(rows * columns). A loop with recursion works too, but a very large region can make the recursion too deep.

problems.title: Pair Count
problems.statement:
A shop has `prices`. A customer wants to buy exactly two different items whose prices add up to exactly `budget`.

Count how many pairs of positions `(i, j)` with `i < j` satisfy `prices[i] + prices[j] == budget`. Two items with the same price at different positions count as different pairs.

examples.explanation: The pairs are (2,4), (3,3) and (1,5).
Any two of the four items work: 4 choose 2 = 6.

hints.nudge: For one price p, which exact price would complete the pair? How could you check that quickly?
hints.pattern: Hash map of counts: how many times each price has appeared so far.
hints.pseudocode:
count = {}; total = 0
for each p in prices:
  total = total + count.get(budget - p, 0)
  count[p] = count.get(p, 0) + 1
return total
hints.walkthrough: Checking every pair is O(n^2), too slow for 50,000 items. Scan left to right keeping a map from price to how many times you have seen it. For the current price p, every earlier item priced budget - p forms a valid pair with it, so add that count to the total. Then record p. Each pair is counted exactly once, when its second item is reached. O(n) time, O(n) space. The result can be over a billion, but fits in a 32-bit int for n <= 50,000.

problems.title: Palindrome List
problems.statement:
Given the head of a singly linked list, return `true` if the values read the same from front to back and from back to front, otherwise `false`. An empty list counts as a palindrome.

A list can only be walked forwards. Can you answer without copying all the values into another list?

examples.explanation: Reading from either end gives 1, 2, 2, 1.
Front to back is 1, 2 but back to front is 2, 1.

hints.nudge: You can compare a front half against a back half if you can walk the back half backwards. How could a list be walked backwards?
hints.pattern: Find the middle with a slow and a fast pointer, reverse the second half in place, then compare the two halves.
hints.pseudocode:
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next: slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next
reverse the list starting at slow (call the new front 'back')
compare head and back node by node until back ends
return true if every pair matched
hints.walkthrough: The easy way copies the values into an array and compares it with its reverse: O(n) time, O(n) memory. To use O(1) extra memory, find the middle node by moving one pointer one step and another pointer two steps at a time: when the fast one reaches the end, the slow one is at the middle. Reverse the part of the list from the middle onwards by turning each next pointer around. Now one pointer walks from the head and another from the new tail of the reversed half; they must show equal values until the reversed half is used up (for an odd length the middle node is compared with itself, which is fine). If you must leave the list as you found it, reverse the second half again afterwards.

problems.title: Palindrome Cuts
problems.statement:
Cut the string `text` into **pieces of consecutive letters** (the pieces together must give back the whole text, in order). A cutting is **good** if **every piece is a palindrome** (reads the same forwards and backwards). For example `aab` can be cut as `a|a|b` or `aa|b`, both good.

Return the **number of good cuttings**.
constraints: text contains only lowercase letters a-z

examples.explanation: a|a|b and aa|b.
a|a|a, a|aa, aa|a, aaa.

hints.nudge: Choose where the first piece ends. It must be a palindrome. What is left to cut afterwards?
hints.pattern: Backtracking over the end of the next piece; or dynamic programming over prefixes.
hints.walkthrough: Recursive version: from a start position, try every end position; if the piece is a palindrome, count the good cuttings of the rest. That recomputes the same suffixes, but with n <= 16 it is still fast. A faster idea: let ways[i] be the number of good cuttings of the first i letters. The last piece covers letters start..i-1; if it is a palindrome, it adds ways[start]. So ways[i] = sum of ways[start] over palindromic pieces ending at i. O(n^2) pieces, each checked in O(n).

problems.title: Count the Palindromic Substrings
problems.statement:
A **substring** is a block of consecutive letters of `text`. A **palindrome** reads the same forwards and backwards.

Return how many substrings of `text` are palindromes. Substrings at different positions count separately, even if they look the same (in `aaa` the single letter `a` counts three times).
constraints: text uses only lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: Only the single letters `a`, `b` and `c`.
`a` three times, `aa` twice and `aaa` once.

hints.nudge: Every palindrome has a middle. If you fix the middle, how far can the palindrome grow?
hints.pattern: Expand around the center: for each of the 2n - 1 possible centers (a letter or the gap between two letters), grow outward while both ends match.
hints.walkthrough: Checking every substring (about n^2 of them) and testing each for a palindrome costs O(n^3). But a palindrome is determined by its middle: for an odd-length palindrome the middle is a letter, for an even-length one it is the gap between two equal letters. There are 2n - 1 such centers. For each center, start with the smallest possible palindrome and keep stepping outward by one letter on each side as long as the two new end letters are equal; every successful step is one more palindromic substring, so add 1 each time. When the ends differ, no larger palindrome can have this center, so stop. O(n^2) time in the worst case (a text of one repeated letter), O(1) extra memory.

problems.title: Read a Number From Text
problems.statement:
Turn the beginning of `text` into a whole number, following these rules in order:
1. Skip any **spaces** at the start (only the space character).
2. If the next character is `+` or `-`, it is the sign (no sign means positive).
3. Read digits until the first character that is not a digit (or the end). Ignore everything after that.
4. If there were no digits, the result is `0`.
5. If the number is outside the range of a 32-bit signed integer (`-2147483648` to `2147483647`), return the nearest end of that range.
constraints: text contains letters, digits, spaces, `+`, `-` and `.`

examples.explanation: Skip the spaces, the sign is `-`, the digits are 42, and `abc` is ignored.
The first character after the (no) spaces is `w`: not a sign and not a digit, so there are no digits.

hints.nudge: Follow the rules like a recipe: one pointer that moves through the text and stops each step when the rule is finished.
hints.pattern: A single left-to-right scan with a position index: spaces, then one optional sign, then digits, building the value as value * 10 + digit.
hints.pseudocode:
i = 0; skip while text[i] == ' '
sign = +1; if text[i] is '+' or '-': remember the sign; i += 1
value = 0
while text[i] is a digit: value = value * 10 + digit; if value > 2147483648: stop; i += 1
result = sign * value; clamp to [-2147483648, 2147483647]
hints.walkthrough: Handle each rule once, moving the index forward and never going back. Skip spaces. Look at one character: if it is a sign, record it and move on (a second sign right after is NOT part of the number, it ends the digits, so `+-12` gives 0). Then read digits while they are digits, multiplying the value so far by 10 and adding the digit. In languages with fixed-size integers the value can overflow while you read a long number: use a 64-bit variable and stop reading as soon as the value is already above 2147483648, since the answer will be clamped anyway. Finally apply the sign and clamp. Remember `-0` is simply 0 and leading zeros do not matter.

problems.title: Split Into Equal Groups
problems.statement:
You are given a list of positive numbers `nums` and a number `k`. Can you divide **all** the numbers into exactly `k` groups (every number goes into exactly one group, and no group is empty) so that **every group has the same sum**?

Return `true` if it is possible, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: The total is 10, which cannot be split into 3 equal sums.

expected.time: O(k^n) worst case, fast with pruning

hints.nudge: If the groups are equal, what must each group's sum be? When is that impossible right away?
hints.pattern: Backtracking: put each number into a group that still has room, undo if it leads nowhere. Prune a lot.
hints.pseudocode:
total = sum(nums); if total % k != 0: return false; target = total / k
sort nums from largest to smallest; if the largest > target: return false
place(i): if i == n: return true
  for each group g (skip a group whose current sum was already tried for this number):
    if group[g] + nums[i] <= target: add; if place(i + 1): return true; undo
  return false
hints.walkthrough: First rule out the easy cases: the total must be divisible by k, and no number may exceed the target sum total / k. Then place the numbers one by one into k groups. Placing the biggest numbers first makes failures show up early. Never put a number into a group that would exceed the target. If two groups currently have the same sum, trying the second one is pointless (it leads to the same situation), so skip it. If every number gets placed, all groups end exactly at the target. A bitmask DP over subsets (2^n states) is another way.

problems.title: Cut Into the Most Pieces
problems.statement:
Cut `text` into **consecutive pieces** (every letter belongs to exactly one piece, and the pieces joined in order give back `text`) so that **no letter appears in more than one piece**.

Return the **largest number of pieces** you can make. The whole text as a single piece is always allowed.
constraints: text uses only lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: `xyx`, `zz` and `wvwuv`: x, y are only in the first piece, z only in the second, w, v, u only in the third.
Cutting anywhere would put an `a` into two pieces.

hints.nudge: If the first letter appears again later, how far must the first piece reach at least? And what if a letter inside it appears even later?
hints.pattern: Remember the LAST position of every letter. Grow the current piece to the farthest last position of any letter inside it; cut when you reach that end.
hints.walkthrough: Trying all ways to cut (2^(n-1)) is far too much. Greedy: the first piece must contain every copy of its first letter, so it reaches at least that letter's last position. Every letter inside the piece pulls the end further out to ITS last position. Keep `end` as the farthest last position seen in the current piece. When the scan reaches position `end`, nothing inside the piece appears later, so you can cut right there and start a new piece. Each cut is made as early as possible, which gives the most pieces. First one pass to store the last position of each letter, then one pass to count the cuts: O(n).

problems.title: Split a List Around a Value
problems.statement:
Rearrange the linked list so that **all nodes with a value less than `pivot` come first**, followed by all nodes with a value **greater than or equal to `pivot`**. Inside each of the two groups the nodes must keep their **original relative order**. Return the head of the rearranged list.

Re-link the existing nodes; do not create new ones.

examples.explanation: Smaller than 3: 1, 2, 2 (in their original order). 3 or more: 4, 3, 5.
1 is smaller than 2 so it moves to the front.

hints.nudge: You do not need to move nodes around inside the list. What if you simply deal the nodes into two separate lists as you walk along?
hints.pattern: Two chains built with dummy head nodes: one for nodes below the pivot, one for the others; at the end join the first chain to the second.
hints.pseudocode:
lessHead, moreHead = dummy nodes; less = lessHead; more = moreHead
for each node in the list:
  if node.val < pivot: less.next = node; less = node
  else: more.next = node; more = node
more.next = null
less.next = moreHead.next
return lessHead.next
hints.walkthrough: Walk through the list once and append every node to the end of one of two chains, depending on its value: chain one for values below the pivot, chain two for the rest. Appending in the order you meet the nodes keeps their original relative order automatically. Dummy first nodes avoid special cases for an empty chain. After the walk you must do two things: end the second chain with an empty next pointer (the last node of the second chain may still point to some old node, which could create a loop), and attach the second chain to the end of the first. The result starts at the first chain's real first node. O(n) time, O(1) extra memory.

problems.title: Trace the Digits
problems.statement:
Every cell of a grid holds a digit. Can the digits in `word` be traced, in order, by moving from cell to cell **up, down, left or right**, without using the same cell twice? The first digit can be found anywhere in the grid.

Return `true` if such a path exists, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: Start at the 1 (top-left), go right to 2, down to 5, down to 8.
The 1 and the 5 touch only diagonally, and diagonal moves are not allowed.

hints.nudge: Try every cell as the start. From a cell that matches the current digit, you have at most 4 places to go. What must you remember so that you never use a cell twice?
hints.pattern: Backtracking (depth-first search with undo): mark a cell as used, try the neighbours for the next digit, then unmark it before trying another route.
hints.pseudocode:
go(r, c, k):
  if grid[r][c] != word[k]: return false
  if k is the last digit: return true
  mark (r, c) used
  for each of the 4 neighbours (nr, nc) inside the grid and not used:
    if go(nr, nc, k + 1): unmark and return true
  unmark (r, c); return false
return true if go(r, c, 0) is true for any cell
hints.walkthrough: Start from every cell that holds the first digit. At each step the current cell must hold the next digit of the word; if it does not, this route is dead and you stop at once (that early stop is what keeps the search small). If it does and it was the last digit, you have a path. Otherwise mark the cell as used, try each unused neighbour for the next digit, and when all of them fail, UNMARK the cell so that other routes may use it later: that undo is what makes it backtracking. Trying every route without stopping early would cost about 4 * 3^(len-1) paths from every cell, while stopping at the first wrong digit usually cuts almost all of them.

problems.title: Is There a Low-High-Middle Pattern
problems.statement: Return `true` if there are three positions `i < j < k` with `numbers[i] < numbers[k] < numbers[j]` (the values form a "1-3-2" shape: a small one, then a big one, then a middle one), otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: The numbers only go up: there is never a smaller number after a bigger one.

hints.nudge: Fix the 'middle' value (the 2) and the 'big' value (the 3) in front of it. Then you only need ONE smaller value even earlier. Scan from the right: what should you remember?
hints.pattern: Scan from right to left with a stack; keep `third`, the largest value that has a bigger value before it (to its left) among those seen; if the current number is smaller than `third`, you found the pattern.
hints.walkthrough: Checking all triples is O(n^3). Going from the right, the stack holds numbers that could play the 'big' part (the 3). When a new number x is bigger than some stack entries, each of those entries has a bigger number (x) to its LEFT and is therefore a valid 'middle' (the 2) for that bigger number; the largest popped entry is the best `third`, because the larger the middle value is, the easier it is to find a smaller number further left. `third` always has a bigger number to its left AND stays to the right of everything still to be read. So when a number x further left is smaller than `third`, the three numbers x, the bigger number and `third` form the pattern in the right order of positions. Each number is pushed and popped at most once: O(n).

problems.title: Count Every Occurrence of a Pattern
problems.statement:
Count how many times `pattern` appears as a block of consecutive letters inside `text`. Occurrences are allowed to **overlap**: in `aaaa` the pattern `aa` appears at positions 0, 1 and 2, which is **3** times.

A slow search compares the pattern with the text at every position and can take `n * m` steps on bad inputs. Aim for time proportional to `n + m`.
constraints: both use only lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: `aba` starts at positions 0, 2 and 4 (the occurrences overlap).
Positions 0, 1 and 2.

hints.nudge: After a mismatch, do you really have to go back and compare the pattern again from the next text position? What do you already know about the letters you have just matched?
hints.pattern: Knuth-Morris-Pratt: precompute, for every prefix of the pattern, the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix; use it to continue after a mismatch without moving back in the text.
hints.pseudocode:
fail[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it
k = 0 (letters matched); count = 0
for each letter ch of the text:
  while k > 0 and ch != pattern[k]: k = fail[k - 1]
  if ch == pattern[k]: k += 1
  if k == len(pattern): count += 1; k = fail[k - 1]
return count
hints.walkthrough: The simple search tries every start position and may re-compare the same text letters many times (for text aaaaaaaaab and pattern aaaaaab it is about n * m steps). KMP never moves backwards in the text. Step 1: for the pattern alone, compute fail[i], the length of the longest prefix of the pattern that is also a suffix of pattern[0..i] (but is shorter than that part). Step 2: scan the text with k = how many pattern letters are currently matched. If the next text letter extends the match, k grows. If not, the pattern letters you matched have a prefix that is also a suffix: instead of starting over, drop to k = fail[k - 1] and try again (repeat until it matches or k is 0). When k reaches the pattern length you found an occurrence; to allow overlaps continue with k = fail[k - 1]. Each text letter makes k grow at most once, and every drop lowers k, so the whole scan is O(n + m).

problems.title: Peak Altitude
problems.statement:
A hiker starts a trail at altitude `0`. The trail is split into segments, and `changes[i]` is the net altitude change over segment `i` (positive = climbing, negative = descending).

Return the **highest altitude** the hiker reaches at any point, including the starting altitude `0`.

examples.explanation: Altitudes are 0, -5, -4, 1, 1, -6. The highest is 1.
The hiker only goes down, so the start (0) is the peak.

hints.nudge: Where is the hiker after segment 1? After segment 2? Try writing the altitudes for the first example.
hints.pattern: This is a running total (prefix sum): keep adding each change to the current altitude.
hints.walkthrough: Start with height = 0 and best = 0 (the start counts). Walk through the list once, adding each change to height. After each step, if height is bigger than best, update best. One pass, no extra memory: O(n) time, O(1) space. Recomputing the sum from the start for every position also works but is O(n^2).

problems.title: Peak Overlap
problems.statement:
A conference hall hosts talks. `talks[i] = [start, end]` means talk `i` runs from time `start` up to, but **not including**, time `end`. So a talk ending at time `t` does not overlap a talk starting at time `t`.

Return the **largest number of talks running at the same moment**.
constraints: talks[i] has exactly two numbers [start, end]

examples.explanation: At time 2 and 3 two talks run. At time 4 the first has ended and two others run.
Each talk ends exactly when the next begins, so they never overlap.
